tagline: River towns, a flood-control reservoir and the protected drop at Cumberland Falls.
intro: The Cumberland Cultural Heritage Highway joins several separate roads across south-central Kentucky. The National Scenic Byway Foundation presents it as a rural journey through mining, railroad and Civil War history, with lakes and rivers offering recreation. It became a state byway in 2001, with a listed length of 187.2 miles. At Campbellsville, access is by two-lane roads.

Road transport changed this region before the heritage designation. Burkesville gained its first major road to Glasgow in 1928; its last steamboat docked the following year. Wolf Creek Dam later impounded the Cumberland River for flood control and hydroelectric power, creating Lake Cumberland. Congress named the impoundment Lake Cumberland in 1952, adopting a name promoted by area business interests.
From Campbellsville, KY 55 runs south to Columbia. The network extends west to Edmonton and east to Russell Springs, with US 127 continuing through Liberty toward Danville and a loop to Stanford.

On the separate southern section, KY 90 starts just south of Burkesville and runs east past the US 127 junctions north of Albany toward Monticello. The designated stretch stops west of Monticello. Farther east, another KY 90 section begins at Parkers Lake and ends at the entrance to DuPont Lodge at Cumberland Falls.

moments.title: Campbellsville
moments.text: Andrew Campbell, who owned a gristmill and tavern, began selling town lots in 1814. Campbellsville’s public square cost the county one dollar. When Taylor County separated from Green County in 1848, the legislature made Campbellsville its seat, and the city sold the square for a courthouse. Confederate cavalry burned that first courthouse in 1864 because Union troops were using it as barracks. A second courthouse followed on the same site after the war. The historic commercial district includes several blocks of Main Street, while a fourth courthouse, the Justice Center, was built on Main Street in 2008.

moments.title: Burkesville
moments.text: Burkesville’s last steamboat docked in 1929, a year after the first major road opened to Glasgow. The town had prospered as a river port in the late nineteenth century, when water transport offered the most feasible way to move bulk goods. Keeping larger river craft moving this far upstream had required diligent dredging of the riverbed to maintain a navigable channel. Wolf Creek Dam, built upstream without a lock, curtailed commercial navigation while controlling floods. River Street still runs directly toward the Cumberland River and the town’s public boat ramp.

moments.title: Albany
moments.text: Albany grew from a tavern established by Benjamin Dowell in the early nineteenth century. Residents chose the location for their county seat in 1837. Formal incorporation followed on January 27, 1838, the year after the vote. The generally accepted namesake is Albany, New York, but a local legend credits tavern patrons calling for Benny during the vote. The Albany-Clinton County Chamber of Commerce carries that story into its annual “All for Benny” dinner on the courthouse square. The town lies at the western edge of the Cumberland Plateau, with Albany Rock rising to the northeast.

moments.title: Cumberland Falls
moments.text: Cumberland Falls drops 68 feet inside the Daniel Boone National Forest. In 1927, discussion of a hydroelectric plant above the falls prompted T. Coleman du Pont to offer to buy the falls and surrounding land for a state park. He died before completing the purchase; his wife bought the falls and 593 surrounding acres in 1930 after the legislature approved the park. The park was dedicated in 1931. The river section containing the falls is designated a Kentucky Wild River, and the park’s forest is a dedicated State Nature Preserve.
moments.notice: On full-moon nights, a moonbow can frequently be seen at the falls.
